utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Call the case, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. This is the case number -- this is the case number IT-99-36-T, the Prosecutor versus Radoslav Brdjanin and Momir Talic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you, Madam Registrar. Mr. Brdjanin, good morning to you. THE ACCUSED BRDJANIN: [Interpretation] Good morning, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Can you hear me in a language that you can understand? THE ACCUSED BRDJANIN: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you. And you may sit down. General Talic, good morning to you, too. Can you hear me in a language that you can understand? THE ACCUSED TALIC: [Interpretation] Good morning, Your Honours. Yes, I can.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you, and you may sit down. Appearances for the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: May it please Your Honours, my name is Andrew Cayley, I appear on behalf of the Prosecutor with Ms. Denise Gustin and Mr. Hasan Younis from the trial support unit. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you. And good morning to you. Appearances for Radoslav Brdjanin.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. I'm John Ackerman. I'm here with Milan Trbojevic and Marela Jevtovic. It's nice to be back.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Good morning to you. Appearances for General Talic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Slobodan Zecevic and Natasha Ivanovic-Fauveau for General Talic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you, and good morning to you. Yes, Mr. Ackerman.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, when I arrived yesterday, I had an opportunity to read the transcript from yesterday's hearing. And I read with interest what Ms. Korner had to say about the AID documents. And I must say that I'm totally baffled at this point. I raised the issue out of an article that appeared in Slobodna Bosna some time ago. The response from the Prosecutor's office was we will look into that. The next thing we heard from the Prosecutor's office was "we have talked with the Prosecutor's office in Sarajevo, and they are sending us a large quantity of material, maybe as much as four boxes. Then the next thing we heard was the four boxes have arrived and we are going through it. And the next thing we heard was those four boxes have nothing to do with the case. Somewhere in there, there is misinformation, I don't know where. But somewhere in there, there is. And I don't know how it happened, but I think Your Honours and the Defence deserve an explanation about that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Cayley.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Mr. President, I think the situation was explained satisfactorily yesterday by Ms. Korner. I certainly understood exactly what was said. The other material that was sent from the government in Sarajevo has absolutely nothing to do with this case. There is a small amount of material, as Ms. Korner stated, that is in connection with the case that Mr. Ackerman raised, and we are going to provide that to the Defence. That's the position.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Zecevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, we are fully joining with what my learned colleague Mr. John Ackerman has just said. The point of the matter if I correctly understand is that we have asked for the certain documents. We are informed by the OTP that these documents have not arrived, but some other documents where in this bunch of documents there are some documents which will be disclosed to us. We are happy with the disclosure of this small amount of documents, but still, the question of the documents which have been requested is still open. Whenever these documents can be given to the Defence, we would very much appreciate any kind of information about that. Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Zecevic, I don't think you are correct in stating that you had requested any particular documents. I mean, the matter was first raised by Mr. Ackerman, and as a response initially, the Prosecution and Mr. Ackerman at that point in time, Mr. Ackerman said that he will be investigating this matter further because all he had was this excerpt or cutting from the Slobodna Bosna. And following that, the Prosecution said that they knew nothing about it, and that they will investigate, too. And next bit of information was what Mr. Ackerman just referred to, that I think it was Ms. Korner who came back at a certain point in time saying that after a question was put once again by Mr. Ackerman weeks later, Ms. Korner said that they had sort of contacted the Sarajevo office, and the matter was being looked into. And as a result, they were informed to expect something like four boxes of documentation. Now, I have no reason to doubt at this point in time, and I don't think either Mr. Ackerman or you have given me -- given us reason to doubt Ms. Korner's statement yesterday that, first, the majority of the documents contained in those boxes belong to another case that has nothing to do with this. That's number one. And secondly, that whatever may be relevant to the case that Mr. Ackerman had referred to in the first place, albeit referring to 1994 or some later date, will be -- and particularly to identity cards, the issue of identity cards will be disclosed to you in the original language because there is this kind of tacit agreement to it. But frankly, things being explained in this manner, I can't see how I can ask for further information. I mean, it may be the only case that -- only thing that I can suggest is for the Prosecution to make certain with the office of the prosecutor in Sarajevo that no further information is in their possession, that this is all that they possessed and all that they have transferred over. And perhaps explain why Ms. Korner in the first place may have been misled into thinking and misleading us into thinking that we were going to have four boxes of material on this -- you may sit down -- pending case in Sarajevo. I don't know. But frankly until I have reason to believe that there is either the Prosecution is not fulfilling its obligations and its duty towards the Defence and towards the Tribunal itself, I don't know what to do frankly except make this suggestion. Yes, Mr. Ackerman.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, please understand I'm not making an accusation against Ms. Korner or Mr. Cayley. I have a question which I think is a legitimate one, and that is how is it that we were told that there was contact with the Prosecutor's office about this matter, and the Prosecutor's office was sending all of the documents, and then we were told they arrived. There were four boxes of them, there were a lot of them. And then yesterday we were told they have nothing to do with this case. How did they get here? Did the Prosecutor's office misunderstand or what?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Probably something like that must have happened, or else -- yes, Mr. Cayley.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Your Honours, one thing I would say, is let's be clear about this, and let's actually address this issue within the rules. That's the context that I would place what Mr. Ackerman is saying. The essential obligation that we have is under Rule 68. Are we in possession of any material which tends to suggest the innocence or mitigate the guilt of the accused or may affect the credibility of Prosecution evidence. That is our obligation. And we address that material on that basis. The bulk of that material has absolutely nothing to do with this case. Now, explaining how we were led to believe that four boxes were relevant to that Prosecution case, I need to speak to other members of staff about whether I can discuss operational issues in this court. But as a general statement, you must understand, we receive a huge amount of material all the time from the Bosnian government. Constantly we are obviously receiving material. But that is the essence of our obligation. We are only obliged to do that. I remember Mr. Ackerman stating last week that it was not for us to decide whether it was relevant. That has absolutely nothing to do with it. Our obligation is to decide whether that material falls within Rule 68, and if it doesn't, then we have no obligation to show that to the Defence. And in this instance, as I say, the bulk of that material has absolutely nothing to do with this case. There is a very small amount of material relating to the Prosecution which Mr. Ackerman first raised and we will disclose that to the Defence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: That's not the point, Mr. Cayley. The point raised by Mr. Ackerman is not that. I would imagine that Mr. Ackerman, if this is the situation, Mr. Ackerman and Mr. Zecevic will have no option but to accept the situation as it is. The whole point that has been made is how come all of a sudden, instead of being told this is the material from the four boxes. We have selected or put aside, selected the wheat from the chaff. This is what we are disclosing to you, but there were four boxes of material. And the information now is yes, there was four -- there were four boxes of material, but these have absolutely nothing to do with the case. The impression that we were given, probably because that was the impression that your office was given from the office in Sarajevo, was that the four boxes being sent contained material relevant to the point raised by Mr. Ackerman. So what Mr. Ackerman is suggesting now or is asking for is whether it is the case of some further inquiry between -- by your office with your corresponding office in Sarajevo to make sure that there is no further material that has been withheld over there and not sent over yet, or that there is not this material in some other four boxes that may have arrived here, but these are not the four boxes that have been opened, or some explanation why you may have in the first place understood that four boxes full of material on this issue were on the way. This is the whole issue. How come that instead of finding four boxes full of material, we found four boxes full of irrelevant material, at least irrelevant as far as this case is concerned.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: As I just stated, Mr. President, it's an operational matter and I will see what I can see. I know what that material is, but I don't know whether I'm in a position to actually state in Court what it is.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I don't think we are interested or Mr. Ackerman is interested in what that material -- other material is. What Mr. Ackerman is interested in knowing, how come this has come about the way it has come about, how come this has happened instead of -- how come that were told to expect four boxes full of material on this Sarajevo pending case issue, and instead it seems that the documents that have arrived have got absolutely nothing to do with that case, bar a few dealing with forgery of identity cards dating to a period which is of no relevance to this case in any case. This is just further -- yes, Mr. Ackerman.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, to now put this in the context of Rule 68 is fine. There's nothing I can do about that. I can't even complain about that but it had not been in that context before. It had been in the context of, what Mr. Ackerman has raised is a very serious matter, Your Honours, and we will investigate it and we will find out what's going on and we will bring that all to you so you will know exactly what the truth of that is. It has now become: No, no, no that's not what we're going to do. What we're going to do is comply with Rule 68. If there's anything that is exculpatory to the Defence we'll give it to them, otherwise, we've completed our burdens in this regard. And that's fine. If the Prosecution wants to take that position I must accept it. But that's different from the initial cooperative position that they took.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, you are right.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And I would like to know if it's possible whether there is any material that hasn't been sent here yet that might fall within even a Rule 68 category, because obviously what they received is not what they were told what they were going to be sent, apparently. But I don't know. This is all mystery to me at this point.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. I think we can close the matter here. I think Mr. Cayley can refer back the whole discussion, the whole debate, basically what needs to be done. And that's with the cooperation of the Prosecution, is to see what brought about this misunderstanding in the first place. And secondly, if behind the -- or beside the misunderstanding, there are further documents that can be made available. That's all. In or outside of the sphere of operation of Rule 68, because Mr. Ackerman is right. The whole idea behind the response of the Prosecution in the first place was not within the -- necessarily within the purview of Rule 68, but it was more open, more generic. Anyway, we can close down the curtains, pull down the curtains. Move into closed session, and bring in the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: be reconvened on Wednesday, the 17th day of July, 2002, at 9.00 a.m. 22 23 24 25
